lesson.title: Beyond the Index: Introducing Dictionaries
lesson.summary: A dictionary stores data as key-value pairs, letting you look up a value by a meaningful label instead of by numeric position.
lesson.body:
Data Types introduced the building blocks Python programs are made of: numbers, strings, booleans, and the containers that hold them. Lists, one of those containers, store values in order and let you retrieve them by position, my_list[0], my_list[1], and so on. That works well when position is meaningful, but plenty of real data isn't naturally ordered by number at all. A student record doesn't have a "position 0" for name and "position 1" for grade in any intuitive sense, it has a name and a grade, labeled by what they are, not by where they sit.

A dictionary solves exactly this problem. Instead of storing values at numbered positions, a dictionary stores values under keys you choose, and you look a value up by that key rather than by counting from the start. Each key maps to exactly one value, called a key-value pair, and a dictionary is written with curly braces containing key: value entries separated by commas.

student = {"name": "Priya", "grade": 11, "gpa": 3.8}
print(student["name"])
print(student["grade"])
print(student)

student["name"] retrieves Priya, and student["grade"] retrieves 11, pulled out by label instead of by position. The final print shows the whole dictionary: {'name': 'Priya', 'grade': 11, 'gpa': 3.8}. Since Python 3.7, dictionaries are guaranteed to preserve the order their key-value pairs were inserted in, so this printed order will always match how the dictionary was written, which is not something sets guarantee.

Keys must be unique within a dictionary, just like elements in a set must be unique, and in fact keys must be hashable for the same underlying reason set elements must be hashable, which is why keys are typically strings, numbers, or tuples rather than lists. Values have no such restriction: a value can be any type at all, including another list or another dictionary. This flexibility is why dictionaries show up constantly in real programs, representing anything from a single student record to an entire configuration file loaded from disk.
